_readme: SEED FILE. `scripts/seed.ts` is the only code path that opens this
directory, and nothing here is read at runtime: Postgres is the
single source of truth once a row lands, so an edit below changes
nothing until the next seed pass applies it.
Keys beginning with an underscore are stripped by the loader before
anything is validated or written, which is what lets a seed file
carry this header at all. A seed is usually met on its own, in a
diff or an editor tab, where nothing about the content says which
path owns it.
This file seeds `topics`. A topic is upserted by the (domain, name)
pair `topics_domain_id_name_unique` holds, so a second seed pass
adjusts a topic's terms and its cadence rather than adding a rival
row on the same subject that would then come due independently.
`domainSlug` is not a column. `topics.domain_id` holds a key the
database issues, and no seed file can know one before the domain
row is written, so a topic names its domain by the only key an
author owns: the slug `domains.json` seeds. The loader resolves it,
and refuses a topic naming a slug the bundle does not carry.
`searchTerms` are queries this topic issues, not the patterns
`terms.json` seeds. A search term goes out to a connector and
decides what the pipeline reads; a term pattern is matched against
what came back and decides how it scores. They are separate columns
on separate tables for that reason, and a phrase that would suit
both is a coincidence rather than a link.
The list is stored so that what will be issued can be read before
it is issued. Terms assembled inside a workflow node are only
visible once a run has already gone out with them, and correcting
them means editing the thing that ran rather than the row that
described it.
`intervalSeconds` is how long this topic waits between runs, and
the two bounds are the range an agent-proposed time is clamped into
before it reaches `next_run_at`. The day, the six-hour floor and
the seven-day ceiling below are illustrative: often enough that a
standing subject stays current, with a floor that stops a proposal
meaning look again shortly from becoming a row that runs every few
seconds, and a ceiling that stops one deferring the topic out of
sight.
Nothing in the database checks those three against each other. No
CHECK relates the bounds to the interval or to `next_run_at`, and
the clamp is the writer's to apply, so an interval outside its own
bounds is storable and refused by nothing. The row below sits
inside its bounds because that is what the example means, not
because anything would report it if it did not.
`nextRunAt` and `enabled` are left out, and both omissions are
deliberate. They are state the dispatcher and the operator own
rather than configuration an author writes, and this file upserts
on every pass: seeding `enabled` would switch a topic back on that
somebody had switched off, and seeding a `next_run_at` would reset
a schedule already in flight. A time is also the one value a seed
cannot know — written here it would be stale before it applied.
So the topic below is configured and not yet due. `next_run_at` is
NULL until something writes one, and the dispatcher arriving in
phase 3 claims by that column, so a seeded topic waits rather than
starting on its own.
One topic, and it is illustrative like the rest of
`example-tech-radar`: broad enough to show what a standing subject
looks like, narrow enough to carry queries of its own, and neutral
about the subject matter. Real subjects belong to whoever operates
an instance and reaches the database through their own seeds.
